newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia PM calls for swift, deep economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia PM calls for swift, deep economic reform.

text.p: Mongolian Prime Minister M. Enkhsaikhan has called for the liberalisation of energy prices and rapid privatisation of state firms to salvage the struggling pastoral nation's economy.
Mongolia needed a sweeping overhaul of its energy prices, privatisation plans, and taxation and welfare systems, Enkhsaikhan told the Great Hural, or parliament, on Friday.

Enkhsaikhan, who was swept to power with the reform-minded Democratic Union Coalition in a suprise election victory in June, accused the previous government of consuming state fuel reserves to the point of endangering national security.
Energy production was dependent on huge state subsidies and was threatening to grind to a halt before the onset of the harsh steppeland winter, he said.

"The inconsistent policies pursued by the previous Great Hural and government have led to shortages of resources, technological obsolescence and made the energy, banking and other sectors vulnerable," he said.
"The seriousness of the situation is such that it is not clear whether the energy sector can survive this winter," he said.
Petrol stations in the capital Ulan Bator raised their prices by up to one third on Sunday, apparently in line with the call for progressive price liberalisation.
Enkhsaikhan pledged to revive a programme of privatisation of manufacturing firms, 85 percent of which were state-owned and whose performance had been stagnant since 1992.
Mongolia's economy has nosedived since the withdrawal in 1991 of Soviet aid that had accounted for about 25 percent of domestic production in the nation of around 2.3 million people.
"We intend to privatise most of manufacturing production and at least 60 percent of all state assets in the coming few years," Enkhsaikhan said.
"We will put an end to the tremendous volume of subsidies being financed by taxpayers and granted to the state enterprises," he said.
The government was also drafting plans to privatise housing by offering homes free of charge or at discounted prices, Enkhsaikhan said.
The privatisation would spur development of small and medium-sized businesses by giving people assets that would make it easier to get bank credit, he said.
A planned overhaul of the tax system would broaden the tax base and shift the burden from investors to consumers. Taxes would be slashed by up to 30 percent, he said.
A fall in income from copper exports from January to July had cut state revenues and bitten deep into the budget.
State revenues totalled 60.6 billion tugriks ($112 million) in the first seven months of 1996 while expenditures were 63.9 billion tugriks, he said.
The new government would try to streamline the welfare system by reducing the number of people on welfare rolls while increasing payments to those still in need of aid, he said.
A recent World Bank report found more than a third of Mongolians were living in poverty, up from 16 percent in 1992.
